stem: A CI system authenticates tens of thousands of short pipeline jobs per hour. Each job reads a few secrets and finishes in minutes, and nothing needs to renew, revoke or create child tokens. Which token type reduces storage load on Vault the most?

choices.text: Batch tokens, because they are encrypted blobs that need no storage writes when they are created.
Root tokens with a use limit, because root tokens bypass the token store when they are generated.
Service tokens with a short TTL, because Vault removes their storage entries immediately after the last use.
Periodic service tokens, because the fixed period lets Vault skip tracking each token in its token store.

stem: Which statement about batch tokens, compared with service tokens, is accurate?

choices.text: A batch token can create child tokens, which expire together with it.
A batch token can be revoked early by looking up its accessor and revoking that accessor.
A batch token is always issued with a fixed TTL and cannot be renewed to extend it.
A batch token can be created as periodic when the role sets a period value.

stem: An application obtained a token with `vault token create -type=batch -ttl=15m`. After ten minutes it runs `vault token renew` and gets an error. What explains the failure?

choices.text: The application first has to call the renewal endpoint with the accessor, which batch tokens return at creation.
Batch tokens can only be renewed after the first half of the TTL has passed, and ten minutes is too early.
The token must be created with the `-period` flag before Vault will accept renewals for it.
Batch tokens are not renewable, so the application must request a new token before the TTL ends.

stem: A platform team runs Vault with performance replication and wants orphan tokens that clients can use against any performance cluster. Which choice fits, and what is the trade-off?

choices.text: Root tokens, accepting that they need a quorum of unseal key holders for every creation.
Batch orphan tokens, accepting that they cannot be renewed or revoked individually.
Periodic service tokens, accepting that the period must be identical on every cluster.
Service tokens, accepting that they are written to storage on every cluster that serves the client.

stem: A release pipeline creates one token per deployment for a deploy agent. The agent must be able to start a helper process that gets its own sub-token, and an operator wants to revoke the agent's access mid-run if needed. Which token fits?

choices.text: A recovery token, because it is the only type meant for short-lived automation.
A service token, because it can create child tokens and can be revoked before it expires.
A batch token with `-orphan`, because orphan batch tokens can create their own children.
A batch token, because an operator can revoke it on its own with `vault token revoke`.

stem: A new administrator asks what makes a root token different from the other tokens a Vault cluster issues. Which statement about root tokens is accurate?

choices.text: A root token has the `root` policy attached and is the only token that can be set to never expire.
A root token always has a 32 day TTL so that a forgotten one revokes itself.
A root token can be created by any token whose policy grants `create` on `auth/token/create`.
A root token is a batch token with an added `root` policy, so it needs no storage.

stem: Which TWO of the following are documented ways to create a root token? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Enabling the `userpass` auth method and assigning the `root` policy to a user.
Running `vault token create -policy=root` with a token that has the `default` policy.
Running `vault login -method=token` with any token that has `sudo` on `auth/token/create`.
Running `vault operator init`, which prints the initial root token.
Running `vault operator generate-root` with a quorum of unseal key holders.

stem: All operators lost the root token, and the production cluster is healthy and unsealed. Which action produces a new root token without restarting Vault?

choices.text: Run `vault token create -policy=root` using any token that has the `admin` policy attached to it.
Run `vault operator init` again so that Vault prints a brand new initial root token for the team.
Start it with `vault operator generate-root -init`, then have key holders submit shares up to the threshold.
Restart the nodes in dev mode so that Vault creates a fresh root token on every startup.

stem: During `vault operator generate-root`, the team passes `-otp=<value>` when they start the attempt. What is the OTP for?

choices.text: It authenticates each unseal key holder, so only people with that code can submit key shares.
It replaces the unseal key threshold, so a single holder can finish the attempt with the OTP.
The final root token is XORed with it, so you recover the real token with `-decode` and the same OTP.
It sets how many seconds the new root token stays valid before it is revoked automatically.

stem: Which practice best matches HashiCorp's guidance for root tokens in a production cluster?

choices.text: Give the root token a short TTL and renew it from a scheduled job so that it stays usable for admins.
Keep a separate root token for each administrator so that audit logs can tell the users apart.
Use a root token for setup or emergencies, revoke it after use, and generate a new one when needed.
Store the initial root token in a shared secret store so any on-call engineer can use it daily.

stem: An admin finishes initial setup using the root token and wants to remove it. Which command revokes the root token currently set in `VAULT_TOKEN`?

choices.text: `vault token renew -increment=0`
`vault operator generate-root -cancel`
`vault operator seal`
`vault token revoke -self`

stem: An auditor sees that every `vault token create` response includes both a `token` and a `token_accessor` field. What is a token accessor?

choices.text: The policy name that Vault attaches to a token so that it can read its own details.
A reference returned at token creation that allows limited actions on the token without exposing its ID.
A second secret that must be sent together with the token to authenticate on every request.
A hash of the token that Vault stores in the audit log as the secret value of the token.

stem: A scheduler creates a token for each job and stores only the accessor. Which TWO actions can it perform later with just that accessor? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Read secrets on behalf of the job by presenting the accessor as the client token.
Revoke the token when the job completes, using `vault token revoke -accessor <accessor>`.
Add new policies to the existing token by supplying the accessor and a policy name.
Print the original token ID again, using `vault token lookup -accessor <accessor>`.
Look up the token's properties, using `vault token lookup -accessor <accessor>`.

stem: A security team needs to list every active token in a Vault cluster for an audit. Which statement about this is accurate?

choices.text: The only way to list tokens is `auth/token/accessors`, which returns accessors rather than tokens.
`vault list auth/token/tokens` returns the token IDs, so auditors can reuse them to log in to Vault.
Vault cannot list tokens, so auditors must parse the audit log for token IDs.
Tokens can be listed only by the root token; every other token gets an empty list.

stem: A developer reads `token_duration 768h` in the output of `vault token create` and asks what the TTL of a Vault service token actually describes. Which is accurate?

choices.text: The time since the token's last use, after which Vault revokes it as inactive.
The total lifetime from creation that can never be extended, no matter how often it is renewed.
The number of times the token can be used before Vault revokes it automatically.
The period of validity since the token's creation or its last renewal, whichever is more recent.

stem: A service token was created with a 1 hour TTL, and the application renews it every 30 minutes. After several weeks a renewal returns a TTL shorter than requested, and later the token stops working. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The 30 minute interval is shorter than the TTL, so Vault treats it as abusive and stops extending.
The token became an orphan, and orphan tokens cannot be renewed after one day.
The token reached the maximum TTL that applies to it, so renewals can no longer extend it.
Vault revokes any token that is renewed more than 48 times in a row.

stem: A token is created with `vault token create -ttl=1h -explicit-max-ttl=4h`. The application renews it each hour. How long can this token live in total?

choices.text: Thirty-two days, because the system max TTL replaces an explicit max TTL.
Indefinitely, because renewing before expiry resets the explicit max TTL each time.
Four hours, because the explicit max TTL is a hard limit that renewals cannot extend.
One hour, because the explicit max TTL applies only if the token is not renewed.

stem: A long-running service keeps a database connection pool and must not lose its Vault token while it is alive, but the token should expire soon after the service is shut down. Which TWO statements about using a periodic token for this are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: If the service stops renewing, the token expires within the period, and its leases are revoked.
Periodic tokens are batch tokens, so renewals are performed by the service without storage.
A periodic token can be created by any token with `create` on `auth/token/create` and no further privileges.
A periodic token can have no TTL at all because the period is only a hint to clients.
Create it with `vault token create -period=2h`; each successful renewal resets the TTL to two hours.

stem: A client received a `403` with `invalid token` and `permission denied` messages when calling Vault with a token that worked yesterday. The token has a 24 hour TTL and was never renewed. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The policy attached to the token was deleted, which turns every call into an invalid token response.
Vault was sealed and unsealed overnight, and sealing deletes all service tokens.
The client IP changed, and Vault answers an unknown source address with `invalid token`.
The token passed its TTL, so Vault revoked it and rejects it as invalid.

stem: During a design review the team debates whether to use orphan tokens for long-lived integrations. Which statement about orphan tokens is accurate?

choices.text: An orphan token is a token whose parent has expired, so Vault immediately revokes it.
An orphan token has no parent, so it is the root of its own tree and is not revoked with other tokens.
An orphan token is a root token without an expiration, created once at `vault operator init` time.
An orphan token can only be a batch token, because service tokens always have a parent.

stem: An engineer logged in with `vault login -method=userpass username=alice` and then ran `vault token create -policy=app` from that session. Later Alice's session token is revoked with `vault token revoke -self`. What happens to the `app` token?

choices.text: It keeps working, because tokens created with `-policy` are always orphans.
Vault revokes it too, because it is a child of the revoked session token.
It keeps working, because only the leases of the parent are revoked.
It becomes an orphan with the same TTL, and an operator must revoke it separately.

stem: A team rotates the token of a deployment service every day by revoking the old token. Each time, tokens created earlier by that service for other apps stop working and the apps fail. Which change fixes this without changing what the apps are allowed to do?

choices.text: Have the service create the app tokens as orphans, via `create-orphan` or a role with `orphan` set.
Give the app tokens a longer TTL than the service token, so they outlive its daily revocation.
Change the app tokens to batch tokens, so that revoking the parent service token leaves them valid.
Attach the `root` policy to the app tokens so that they no longer depend on the service token.

stem: A platform engineer is reviewing how tokens end up without a parent in a Vault cluster. Which TWO actions create an orphan token? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Writing to `auth/token/create-orphan` with a token whose policy allows it.
Running `vault token create -use-limit=1` with an ordinary child token.
Running `vault token create -policy=app` with a token that is allowed to create child tokens.
Running `vault token renew` on a child token before its parent expires.
Logging in with an auth method other than `token`, such as `userpass`.

stem: A team wants a token for a scheduler that must have only the `batch-jobs` policy, with no `default` policy. Which command creates it?

choices.text: `vault token create -policy=batch-jobs -type=batch`
`vault token create -policy=batch-jobs -orphan`
`vault token create -policy=batch-jobs -no-default-policy`
`vault token create -policy=batch-jobs -use-limit=0 -renewable`

stem: A deployment script needs a credential that works for exactly one request to Vault, then dies. Which creation option provides that?

choices.text: `-renewable=false`
`-use-limit=1`
`-explicit-max-ttl=1`

stem: A team plans to standardize token creation for CI jobs by defining a token store role named `ci`. Which statement about token store roles is accurate?

choices.text: A role can only be used by a root token, because creating against any role always needs `sudo` on the path.
A role at `auth/token/roles/ci` is used with `vault token create -role=ci` and can override request parameters.
A role replaces the `default` policy and must be written in HCL like a policy.
A role stores a token itself, so every `-role=ci` call returns the same token value.

stem: An operator wants workers to create their own tokens for a monitoring job, and these tokens must be periodic and orphan, but workers must not get `sudo` on `auth/token/create`. Which design fits?

choices.text: A role with `period` and `orphan` set, plus a policy allowing `update` on `auth/token/create/monitor`.
A batch token role, because batch tokens can be periodic and orphan when created from a role.
Give workers a policy with `sudo` on `auth/token/create` so they can pass `-period` and `-orphan` themselves.
A shared root token that workers use to create tokens, revoked at the end of every day.

stem: Running `vault token create -period=1h` as a developer returns `permission denied`, while `vault token create -policy=app` works. What explains it?

choices.text: Periodic tokens can only be created with the `-type=batch` flag.
The `-period` flag requires the developer to supply an explicit max TTL as well.
Developers cannot create periodic tokens because periodic tokens are reserved for the `root` policy only, even with `sudo`.
Setting a period needs `sudo` on the create path (or a root token), which the developer's policy lacks.

stem: An application runs `vault read database/creds/readonly` and gets a username, a password and a long identifier. Which value does the application keep so that it can later renew or revoke these credentials?

The token accessor, because it names the credential issued by the read request

choices.text: The prefix is always the mount type, so every lease of one engine type shares an identical ID prefix

Policies attached to an auth method role

stem: An engineer lost the lease ID of database credentials issued from `database/creds/readonly` and wants to find it from the CLI. Which approach works?

It prints the secret's username and password again from the stored lease record

`POST /v1/sys/leases/lookup` with the `lease_id` in the JSON body

The server needs a policy for the original secret path, because unwrapping rechecks that policy
Someone may already have unwrapped it, so a security investigation should start using audit logs
Vault has lost the wrapped data because response-wrapping tokens are cached in memory only

stem: A secret was wrapped, and the receiving team wants to check where it came from before unwrapping. Which action supports this?

choices.text: Look up the wrapping token and compare its creation path with the path they expect, such as pki/issue/web
Check the signature on the wrapping token, which Vault signs with its public key for this reason
Read the secret with the token first, then wrap it again to a new token and compare creation times
Ask Vault to list the cubbyhole of the wrapping token to find the original request path

stem: Which TWO benefits does response wrapping give when a secret travels through an intermediate system? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The wrapped secret inherits the TTL of the original lease and cannot be shortened
Logs along the way contain only a reference token and not the secret value
Any holder of the token can unwrap it repeatedly until the original lease ends
The wrapped secret itself is re-generated by the engine at every unwrap
Only one party can ever unwrap the token, so interception can be detected

stem: What is the main security value of short-lived, dynamically generated credentials, compared with one shared long-lived password?

choices.text: A credential never needs to be revoked, because Vault deletes all copies from client memory at expiry
A leaked credential can be used only from the network that requested it, because Vault binds it to a source address
A credential is only valid for one read, so no application can use the same value twice
A leaked credential is valid only for a short time, and each consumer has a unique identity that makes tracing easier

stem: A platform team argues about certificate TTLs for service-to-service TLS issued by the PKI engine. Which approach matches the engine's documented design?

choices.text: Keep TTLs short so revocation is rarely needed, CRLs stay small and each instance gets its own certificate
Share one certificate among all instances of a service, so the CRL keeps a single entry per service
Issue certificates with the longest TTL the role allows, so clients rarely have to request new ones
Write issued certificates and private keys to disk, so that instances reuse them after a restart

stem: An operator wants a versioned KV engine at secret-apps/ and runs vault secrets enable -path=secret-apps -version=2 kv. Which statement about the result is accurate?

choices.text: The command fails, because the path of a kv engine must be named secret
The command mounts the kv engine in version 2 mode at secret-apps/, and kv-v2 as the type name gives the same result
The command mounts a version 1 engine, because the version of the engine can only be set later through the UI
The command mounts kv at secret-apps/ and the data is then reachable at secret-apps/ plus the key, with no data/ segment

stem: An operator runs vault secrets tune -max-lease-ttl=30m db-prod/. What does this do?

choices.text: It changes the maximum lease TTL setting of the mount at db-prod/ without moving or disabling the engine
It moves the engine to db-prod/ and shortens its leases as a side effect
It changes the maximum token TTL for all auth methods across the cluster
It shortens every lease already issued by db-prod/ to expire in 30 minutes from the command

stem: Which TWO statements about enabling secrets engines are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The same mount can be created from the UI only, while the CLI and API cannot enable engines
A mount path may be changed freely after enabling without affecting issued leases
Every engine type can be enabled at only one path per cluster
The kv/ and KV/ paths are two different mounts, because mount paths are case-sensitive
Without -path an engine mounts at its type name, so aws is enabled at aws/

stem: A script uses vault kv get -mount=secret creds against a KV v2 engine and the team now wants the same read through curl. Which request does it correspond to?

choices.text: A GET to /v1/secret/data/creds with the X-Vault-Token header
A POST to /v1/sys/mounts/secret/creds with the X-Vault-Token header
A GET to /v1/secret/creds with the X-Vault-Token header
A GET to /v1/secret/metadata/creds with the X-Vault-Token header

stem: A developer deleted the latest version of a KV v2 secret with vault kv delete -mount=secret creds by mistake. What should the operator do to bring it back?

choices.text: Run vault kv undelete for that version, since delete marks the version as deleted
Run vault kv metadata delete, which restores the deleted versions of the key
Nothing, because a KV v2 delete removes the underlying data of the version
Run vault kv destroy for the version, which re-creates the version data from storage

stem: An application must change only the api-token field of a KV v2 secret at secret/web-app that also holds a second field, region. Which command keeps region untouched?

choices.text: vault kv enable-versioning -mount=secret web-app, which turns on version history for the secret
vault kv put -mount=secret web-app api-token=NEW, which merges the field into the current version
vault kv patch -mount=secret web-app api-token=NEW, which merges the field into the current version
vault kv rollback -mount=secret web-app, which restores the previous version of the secret

stem: On a KV version 2 mount at secret/, an operator wants the same result as vault kv get -mount=secret creds but must use the generic vault read command. Which command works?

choices.text: vault read secret/data/creds, because the generic command needs the real API path that includes the data/ segment
vault read secret/creds, because the generic command adds the data/ segment on its own for KV version 2 mounts
vault read secret/metadata/creds, because the metadata path returns the current value of the secret
vault read secret/creds/data, because the data/ segment follows the key name in KV version 2 paths

stem: An application must encrypt the string `4111 1111 1111 1111` with the key `orders` from the CLI. Which command is correct?

choices.text: `vault write transit/encrypt/orders plaintext="4111 1111 1111 1111"`
`vault write transit/encrypt/orders plaintext=$(echo -n "4111 1111 1111 1111" | base64)`
`vault write transit/orders/encrypt plaintext=$(echo -n "4111 1111 1111 1111" | base64)`
`vault write transit/encrypt/orders ciphertext=$(echo -n "4111 1111 1111 1111" | base64)`

stem: Vault returns the ciphertext `vault:v1:8SDd3W...`. What does the `v1` segment tell Vault?

choices.text: That the ciphertext was produced by the first version of the transit engine API.
That the key is a version 1 key type, which cannot be upgraded after a later rotation.
That the value is the first of a numbered series of ciphertexts from the same key.
That key version 1 in the key ring encrypted the plaintext, so decryption uses that version.

stem: A developer runs `vault write transit/decrypt/orders ciphertext=vault:v1:8SDd3W...`, and the output shows `plaintext  bXkgc2VjcmV0IGRhdGEK`. Their application expected `my secret data`. What is the correct next step?

choices.text: Call the rewrap endpoint, which converts the decrypted value into readable text for the caller.
Rotate the `orders` key, because the output shows that the ciphertext was decrypted with a stale version.
Base64-decode the returned plaintext, because transit always returns decrypted data base64-encoded.
Re-run the command with `-format=json`, which makes Vault return the plaintext in its original form.

stem: An operator runs `vault write -f transit/keys/orders/rotate`. A record encrypted yesterday is `vault:v1:...`. What happens next?

choices.text: The existing `vault:v1:` record stops decrypting, and it works again only after an operator rewraps it to the new version.
New encryptions use the new key version, and the old `vault:v1:` record still decrypts via the key ring.
Vault re-encrypts every stored record on its own and replaces the old prefix with `vault:v2:`.
New encryptions keep using version 1 until the application passes `key_version=2` explicitly on each request.

stem: Which TWO statements about the transit rewrap endpoint are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The caller supplies ciphertext and receives new ciphertext produced with the latest key version.
The endpoint decrypts with the latest key version and re-encrypts with the oldest version.
The endpoint rotates the named key before re-encrypting, so each call adds a key version.
The caller receives the plaintext only if the policy also allows decrypt on the same key.
A token allowed to call rewrap can safely be given to an untrusted process, as the plaintext is never returned.

stem: After rotating the `customers` key, a security team must move 20 million stored `vault:v1:` values to the new key version. The batch job must never be able to read customer data. What is the best design?

choices.text: Give the job decrypt and encrypt on the key, then have it re-encrypt each value with the newest key version.
Give the job read on `transit/keys/customers` so it can export the key and re-encrypt locally.
Delete the old key version so Vault re-encrypts remaining values the next time they are read.
Give the job only update on `transit/rewrap/customers` and have it store each returned ciphertext.

stem: A key `orders` has versions 1 to 4. An operator sets `min_decryption_version` to 3 after old backups containing `vault:v1:` values leaked. What happens to those leaked values and to the data?

choices.text: Vault rewraps the v1 and v2 values to version 4 when they are next decrypted.
Only `vault:v1:` values stop decrypting, since version 2 is always kept in the working set as a fallback.
The `vault:v1:` and `vault:v2:` values stop decrypting, and the setting can be lowered again in an emergency.
Versions 1 and 2 are permanently deleted from the key ring, so those leaked values can never be recovered.

stem: A key has versions 1 to 5. An operator sets `min_encryption_version` to 4 on the key. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: The value must be lower than the current `min_decryption_version`, or the API rejects the change.
Decryption of ciphertext that was made with key versions 1 to 3 is now blocked for all callers.
Encryption may only use version 4 or later, and unpinned requests still use the latest version.
Versions 1 to 3 are permanently removed from the key ring once the new setting is saved.

stem: A team wants to remove key versions 1 and 2 permanently so that nobody can ever recover them, even in an emergency. Which action does that?

choices.text: Set `min_decryption_version` to 3, which erases older versions after a short grace period.
Call `transit/keys/<name>/trim` with `min_available_version` set to 3.
Set `deletion_allowed` to true and call the delete endpoint, which removes only the oldest versions.
Rotate the key twice more, since each rotation overwrites the oldest version.

stem: An operator runs `vault delete transit/keys/legacy` and gets an error even though the token has `delete` on the path. What is the most likely reason?

choices.text: The key has `deletion_allowed` set to false, so the operator must enable it in the key's config first.
The key was created with `exportable=true`, which blocks deletion until export is disabled.
The transit engine must be disabled first, since single keys can be removed only with the mount.
The key must be rotated first, because a key can be deleted only after it has more than one version.

stem: A team needs a transit key to encrypt and decrypt application records. Which key type fits?

choices.text: `hmac`, because the keyed value it produces can later be reversed to recover the original plaintext.
`ecdsa-p256`, because elliptic-curve keys can encrypt records and are quick to use in practice.
`ed25519`, because it supports key derivation, so it can encrypt per-tenant records.
`aes256-gcm96`, the default key type, which supports encryption, decryption, derivation and convergent encryption.

stem: Which TWO transit key types support convergent encryption? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `aes128-gcm96`, AES-GCM with a 128-bit key and a 96-bit nonce
`rsa-4096`, a 4096-bit RSA key that can encrypt and sign data
`ed25519`, a signing key type that supports key derivation
`ecdsa-p384`, an ECDSA key that uses the NIST curve P-384
`chacha20-poly1305`, a ChaCha20-Poly1305 key of 256 bits

stem: A customer table stores encrypted email addresses, and the application must run `WHERE email = ?` without decrypting the column. Which transit setup supports this?

choices.text: A default key, as every encryption of the same email returns the same ciphertext.
A key rotated daily, so equal emails produce matching ciphertext within one rotation window.
A key with `exportable=true`, so the application can hash the email itself before it queries the table.
A key created with `derived=true` and `convergent_encryption=true`, encrypting each email with a fixed context.

stem: An engineer runs `vault write transit/keys/emails type=aes256-gcm96 convergent_encryption=true` and the request fails. What is the cause?

choices.text: Convergent encryption is supported only by `aes128-gcm96`, so the type must be changed.
Convergent encryption requires key derivation, so the key must also be created with `derived=true`.
Convergent encryption requires `exportable=true` so that the nonce can be read back by clients.
Convergent encryption must be enabled by the first encrypt call and cannot be given at creation.

stem: A SaaS provider encrypts data for many tenants with one transit key and wants each tenant's data protected by a different effective key. Which feature does this?

choices.text: Setting `min_encryption_version` to a different value for each tenant before encrypting that tenant's data.
Enabling `allow_plaintext_backup`, so each tenant has its own backup of the key to restore from.
Creating the key with `derived=true`, then passing each tenant's own base64 `context` on every encrypt and decrypt.
Using the `rewrap` endpoint to assign a tenant tag to each ciphertext.

stem: Which statement describes where the data lives when an application uses the transit secrets engine?

choices.text: Vault does not store the data; the app keeps the ciphertext in its own datastore and sends it back to decrypt.
Vault stores the encrypted data in its storage backend and returns it when the application asks.
Vault keeps the plaintext in memory for a lease period so that the app can request it again.
Vault stores the ciphertext only until the application confirms receipt, then deletes it.

stem: A team wants developers to stop writing their own cryptographic code in each service while data stays in the existing PostgreSQL database. Which approach matches the stated primary use case of transit?

choices.text: Developers fetch the key from Vault and run their own AES code locally on each sensitive field.
Developers store each field in the KV engine and keep a reference to its path in PostgreSQL.
Developers request a short-lived dynamic database credential from Vault for each row they protect.
Developers call Vault to encrypt a field and store the ciphertext in PostgreSQL; operators manage keys.

stem: An application should be able to encrypt and decrypt with the `orders` key and nothing else in transit; operators manage keys separately. Which policy stanzas meet this?

choices.text: Paths `transit/encrypt/orders` and `transit/decrypt/orders`, each with only the `read` capability.
Path `transit/*` with the `read` capability, since reading a key allows its use.
Path `transit/keys/orders` with the `update` capability, which covers encrypt and decrypt.
Paths `transit/encrypt/orders` and `transit/decrypt/orders`, each with the `update` capability.

stem: An application signed a message with the `ecdsa-p256` key `signer` by calling `transit/sign/signer` with base64 `input`, and stored the returned `vault:v1:...` signature. Which CLI call checks that signature later?

choices.text: `vault write transit/sign/signer input=<base64 message> signature=<signature>`, which compares the new signature to the stored one.
`vault write transit/verify/signer input=<base64 message> signature=<signature>`
`vault write transit/decrypt/signer ciphertext=<signature>`, which returns the signed message when the signature is valid.
`vault write transit/verify/signer plaintext=<base64 message> signature=<signature>`

stem: An operator enables automatic rotation of a transit key with `vault write transit/keys/orders/config auto_rotate_period=720h`. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Vault rejects 720h, because the config endpoint refuses rotation periods shorter than 90 days.
Vault deletes and recreates the key each 720 hours, so existing ciphertext has to be rewrapped first.
Vault re-encrypts the stored ciphertext on that schedule and updates its `vault:vN:` version prefix.
Vault adds a key version about every 720 hours; new data uses it while older ciphertext still decrypts.

stem: A service's token has only the `update` capability on `transit/encrypt/*`. It calls `transit/encrypt/newkey`, and no key named `newkey` exists. What happens?

choices.text: The call fails, because creating a missing key through the encrypt path needs `create`, not `update`.
The call fails, because transit keys must be created at `transit/keys/newkey` before encrypt is called.
The call succeeds if the request also passes `type=aes256-gcm96`, which tells transit which key to create.
The call succeeds and creates `newkey` with default settings, since `update` covers writes to the path.

stem: A key was created with `exportable=false` (the default) and later an auditor asks for it to be exportable. After an operator sets `exportable=true` on the key config, the auditor asks to set it back to false. What is the outcome?

choices.text: The setting cannot be switched back to false; once enabled it stays enabled for that key.
The operator can switch it back, but only after the key has been rotated at least once.
The setting resets by itself as soon as the first export of the key has finished.
The operator can switch it back by using a token with `sudo` on the key's config path.

stem: An import job must encrypt 5,000 small values. Which approach reduces round trips while keeping results matched to inputs?

choices.text: Send one request with a comma-separated `plaintext` string; Vault splits it and returns one ciphertext.
Rotate the key before each value so that every ciphertext has its own version.
Open one lease on the key and reuse its lease ID for 5,000 encrypt calls.
Send one request with `batch_input`, a list of items; the response keeps the order of the input.

stem: Which statement about the transit engine's other cryptographic functions is accurate?

choices.text: Transit can sign data with an `aes256-gcm96` key, since signing uses the same key material as encryption.
Transit can hash data and generate random bytes, but signing and verification need the PKI engine instead.
Transit random bytes are returned after the caller names an existing encryption key in the request path.
Transit can generate random bytes, hash data and compute HMACs, and keys such as `ecdsa-p256` can sign data.

stem: An application wants a fresh data key per file so it can encrypt large files locally, with a copy of each key that only Vault can open. Which TWO statements about the transit data key endpoints are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The encrypted copy of a data key can be opened only by calling rewrap, never by calling decrypt.
`transit/datakey/wrapped/files` returns only the encrypted copy, which a trusted caller can later send to decrypt.
Both datakey paths store the generated key in Vault so that it can be read again later by the same token.
`transit/datakey/wrapped/files` returns the plaintext key once and then deletes it from Vault memory after use.
`transit/datakey/plaintext/files` returns the key in plaintext together with a copy encrypted by the named key.

stem: Which TWO statements are trade-offs of using transit instead of encrypting inside each application with a local library? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Every encrypt or decrypt becomes a network request, so the application depends on Vault being reachable.
Transit makes the ciphertext format independent of key rotation, so no rewrap is ever needed.
Transit stores a copy of every encrypted value, which increases Vault storage use over time.
Transit requires each application to implement its own key rotation, as Vault cannot rotate keys.
Transit keeps keys, rotation and audit logging in one place, while applications never hold the key.

stem: An application encrypted a value with the key `orders` and later sends the ciphertext to `transit/decrypt/payments`, which fails. What is the cause?

choices.text: Decrypt endpoints accept only ciphertext that was created earlier by the very same client token.
The payments key must be rotated once before it is able to read ciphertext made by other keys.
Ciphertext is bound to its key, so only `orders` can decrypt it.
The ciphertext prefix `vault:v1:` must first be edited to read `vault:payments:` before the call.

stem: An auditor with read access runs `vault read transit/keys/orders` hoping to collect the AES key behind the `orders` key. What does the response contain?

choices.text: The key metadata, such as type, versions with creation times and the minimum versions, but not the key material.
Every key version in base64, because read access to the key path is what allows the key to be exported.
Only the latest key version in plaintext, with older versions shown as hashes in the response.
An error, because symmetric keys cannot be read at all, not even to see their settings or versions.

stem: A team runs a self-managed Vault cluster with Integrated Storage on five nodes. Two nodes fail at the same time because of a rack power loss. What is the state of the cluster?

choices.text: The remaining three nodes lose quorum, because a five-node Raft cluster needs four voters to commit writes
The remaining three nodes stay available if the failed pair held fewer than the threshold of unseal key shares
The remaining three nodes turn read-only until the failed peers are removed with a raft remove-peer command
The remaining three nodes still form a quorum, so the cluster keeps electing a leader and committing writes

stem: An architect proposes growing a three-node Integrated Storage cluster to four nodes "for more resilience". Which statement about this change is accurate?

choices.text: Four nodes raise failure tolerance to two, since the extra node can vote on behalf of a failed peer
Four nodes keep failure tolerance at one, so the extra node adds cost and no extra fault tolerance
Four nodes lower failure tolerance to zero because Raft needs an odd number of nodes to elect a leader
Four nodes keep failure tolerance at one and also double read throughput, because standbys serve reads

stem: A two-node Integrated Storage cluster was built for a lab. One node crashes. The remaining node still answers `vault status` but cannot accept writes. What explains this?

choices.text: The surviving node lacks the Enterprise license that is needed to run a cluster of fewer than three
The surviving node sealed itself automatically, since a Shamir seal requires both nodes to stay online
The peer set of two has a quorum of two, so one node alone cannot commit entries or elect a leader
The surviving node is a standby that never held the HA lock, so it must wait for the lease to expire

stem: A cluster of three Vault nodes shares one storage backend that supports high availability. Which statement about how the nodes behave is accurate?

choices.text: Writes go to all nodes at once, and each node signs its replies so that clients accept the first one
Every node serves reads and writes in parallel, and the load balancer should spread requests evenly
One node holds the HA lock and is active, while the others are standbys that forward or redirect requests to it
One node is active, and a standby only starts forwarding after an operator unseals it with the root key

stem: A three-node HA cluster uses auto-unseal. Two standbys were restarted by an automated patch job and an operator ran `vault operator seal` on them for testing, so they are sealed. The active node then crashes. What happens?

choices.text: A sealed node takes the HA lock and unseals itself with the KMS, which restores service within seconds
The third node continues alone because Raft quorum counts only nodes that run an unsealed process
The cluster promotes the sealed nodes, which answer read requests from their local copy of the data
The cluster stays unavailable because sealed servers cannot act as standbys or take over as active

stem: In a Vault Enterprise HA cluster, administrators enable performance standby nodes. Which statement about their role is accurate?

choices.text: They replace the HA lock, so any performance standby can answer writes without contacting the active node
They serve requests that do not modify storage and forward requests that need a write to the active node
They are separate clusters in another region that hold a copy of the data and serve only disaster recovery
They accept all writes locally and later replicate them to the active node through a replication token

stem: Which TWO statements about Autopilot in a self-managed Integrated Storage cluster are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Dead server cleanup can remove unhealthy nodes from the Raft cluster without an operator doing it manually
Autopilot converts a standby into an active node when the stability threshold is set to zero seconds
Autopilot is available only if the cluster is configured with Consul as an external storage backend
Autopilot replaces the Shamir seal so that new nodes join without any unseal key or recovery key
A newly joined node becomes a non-voter until it has synced and reached the configured stability threshold

stem: A company is designing a new self-managed Vault cluster and has no existing Consul infrastructure. Which choice matches HashiCorp's recommendation for the storage backend?

choices.text: A local file backend on each node, with a shared network drive so that every node reads the same files
Consul, because only a separate Consul cluster supports high availability with a lock in the data store
Integrated Storage, since it needs no extra software, keeps data on the Vault hosts and is HashiCorp supported
Integrated Storage on the active node and an external database on the standbys for faster read access

stem: Which TWO statements correctly compare Consul as Vault's storage backend with Integrated Storage? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Consul has a larger maximum entry size than Integrated Storage, which is why it suits large secrets
Integrated Storage needs only the Vault cluster, while Consul needs a Vault cluster plus a Consul cluster
A Consul cluster that stores Vault data should also run service mesh so the data is shared with applications
Consul removes the need to unseal Vault, because the Consul ACL token decrypts the stored data
Consul keeps all Vault data in memory, so it needs more frequent snapshots than an on-disk store

stem: A config uses `storage "s3"` for data and `ha_storage "consul"` for the lock. What does the split provide?

choices.text: The S3 bucket acts as the leader, and Consul replicates the S3 data to a secondary cluster in another region
The S3 bucket holds the unseal keys, while Consul holds the encrypted data and replicates to standbys
The S3 bucket stores audit logs for compliance, while Consul stores the token and lease records only
The S3 bucket holds Vault's encrypted data, while Consul holds the HA lock that picks the active node

stem: An operator runs `vault operator init -key-shares=5 -key-threshold=3` on a new self-managed cluster with a Shamir seal. Two of the five key holders leave the company. Can the cluster still be unsealed?

choices.text: No, because the threshold counts shares held by the original group of five named key holders
Yes, because three remaining holders meet the threshold, whatever order they enter shares in
Yes, once the two missing shares have been regenerated with a command run on an unsealed node
No, because the unseal key is rebuilt from the full set of five shares created at initialization

stem: A new node must join an existing three-node Integrated Storage cluster whose leader listens at `https://vault-1.example.com:8200`. Which command, run on the new node, starts the join?

`vault operator unseal -join https://vault-1.example.com:8200`
`vault operator raft peers add https://vault-1.example.com:8200`
`vault operator raft join https://vault-1.example.com:8200`

stem: Two key holders leave a company that runs a Shamir-sealed cluster with five shares and a threshold of three. Which TWO statements about rekeying the unseal key with `vault operator rekey` are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The old shares keep working next to the new ones until the nodes of the cluster are restarted
It re-encrypts the secrets in the storage backend, so its duration grows with the size of the data
The cluster has to be sealed first, because new shares are not created while the data is readable
It is authorized by submitting the current threshold number of unseal key shares from existing holders
It can set a new share count and threshold, and the new shares can be handed to different holders

stem: A security team is reviewing how the default Shamir seal protects a self-managed cluster. Which statement about it is accurate?

choices.text: The threshold of shares is combined to reconstruct the unseal key, which is then used to decrypt the root key
A Shamir seal fits large dynamic clusters well, since nodes automatically unseal after every restart
Shamir shares are stored in the storage backend so that standby nodes can rebuild the key themselves
A single share is enough to decrypt data, provided the holder has a root token for the cluster

stem: A platform team runs dozens of Vault clusters in autoscaling groups, and nodes are replaced several times per week. Why does the team move from a Shamir seal to auto-unseal?

choices.text: Auto-unseal makes unseal keys unnecessary by storing them in the data store next to the encrypted secrets
A trusted external service such as a cloud KMS decrypts the root key at start, so nodes unseal without human operators
A node with auto-unseal no longer needs a storage backend, because the KMS holds the encrypted data
Auto-unseal removes the root key from the design, so there is no key to protect, only the policies

stem: An operator initializes a cluster that uses a cloud KMS for auto-unseal. The output lists five recovery key shares. For which task are the recovery keys used?

choices.text: Authorizing quorum operations such as generating a root token, in place of Shamir unseal keys
Unsealing a node when the KMS is unavailable, as a replacement for the unseal keys
Signing the replication token that links a performance secondary to a primary cluster
Decrypting the root key offline so a backup of the storage backend can be restored

stem: A self-managed cluster uses a cloud KMS key for auto-unseal. During cleanup an administrator schedules that KMS key for permanent deletion, before any seal migration. The nodes are still running. What is the risk?

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the five recovery key shares can unseal the cluster if the KMS key disappears
Vault re-encrypts the root key with the Shamir algorithm at once and prints new unseal keys to the audit log
The cluster remains usable, but the stored secrets become readable only through the root token

stem: A cluster uses auto-unseal and the security team wants new key holders for the recovery key. Which command changes the recovery key share count and threshold?

choices.text: `vault operator unseal -migrate -recovery`
`vault operator rotate -target=recovery`
`vault operator rekey -target=recovery`
`vault operator generate-root -target=recovery`

stem: Vault 1.19 runs on virtual machines outside Kubernetes. stem: An on-call engineer, mlee, logs in with userpass. stem: A self-managed Vault Community cluster was built with five Integrated Storage voters. Last week the autoscaling group replaced vault-d and vault-e, and their replacements vault-f and vault-g joined through retry_join. Autopilot runs with its default configuration. Today `vault operator raft list-peers` shows seven entries, all with Voter true: vault-a (leader), vault-b, vault-c, vault-f and vault-g, plus vault-d and vault-e, whose instances no longer exist. The team believes the cluster still tolerates two node failures. It must tolerate two failures again, and future replacements must be cleaned up without manual steps. What should the operator do?

choices.text: Run vault operator raft remove-peer for vault-d and vault-e, then set cleanup_dead_servers=true with min_quorum=5 in the autopilot configuration
Make no change, because peers whose instances no longer exist are left out of the quorum count, so five live voters still tolerate two failures
Run vault operator raft remove-peer for vault-d and vault-e, then set dead_server_last_contact_threshold=1m so that replacements are pruned fast
Set cleanup_dead_servers=true in the autopilot configuration and leave min_quorum unset, so autopilot prunes vault-d, vault-e and later dead nodes

stem: A Vault Enterprise customer has a primary cluster in us-east, a performance secondary in eu-west and a disaster recovery secondary in us-west. A regional outage takes us-east offline for several days. Applications in the US hold service tokens and database leases issued by us-east, and the business requires that they continue without re-authenticating. The eu-west cluster has more capacity and is closer to the operations team, who suggest using it. The operators can obtain a DR operation token for the us-west cluster. Which plan restores service for the US applications as required?

choices.text: Promote the eu-west performance secondary to primary, because it already serves client requests and holds copies of the primary's tokens and leases
Point the US applications at the us-west DR secondary without promoting it, because DR secondaries answer read requests while the primary is down
Promote the us-west DR secondary to primary, then have every US application log in again, because DR secondaries replicate configuration only
Promote the us-west DR secondary to primary with a DR operation token, because it mirrors the tokens and leases and serves clients once promoted

stem: A legacy reporting tool on a VM cannot be modified. It sends every Vault API request to a local Vault Agent listener at 127.0.0.1:8100 and always attaches an `X-Vault-Token` header holding a token that was hard-coded years ago and has long expired. Agent uses AppRole auto-auth successfully, its file sink holds a valid token, the AppRole role carries the tool's policies, and the `api_proxy` stanza sets `use_auto_auth_token = true`. The tool's requests still fail with permission errors. Only this tool uses this listener. Which change makes the tool's requests succeed?

choices.text: Set use_auto_auth_token = false in api_proxy, so that Agent stops adding its own token and passes the request's header to Vault unchanged instead
Keep use_auto_auth_token = true and add a cache stanza, so that Agent answers the tool's requests from responses cached with the auto-auth token
Set use_auto_auth_token = "force" in api_proxy, so that Agent ignores the expired token on each request and forwards it with the auto-auth token
Keep use_auto_auth_token = true and point the tool's VAULT_TOKEN variable at the sink file, so that the tool sends Agent's valid token instead

stem: A VaultStaticSecret syncs the KV v2 secret `web/config` into the Kubernetes Secret `web-config` with refreshAfter: 30s, and lists the Deployment `web` under rolloutRestartTargets because the application reads its values only at start-up. To avoid storing a data MAC in the resource status, an engineer set hmacSecretData: false last month. Today an operator changed the secret in Vault; within a minute `kubectl get secret web-config -o yaml` shows the new values, but the web pods were never restarted and still use the old configuration. Nothing else changed. Which change makes VSO restart the Deployment on future secret changes?

choices.text: Lower refreshAfter to 5s, because the operator restarts targets only when it notices a change within one refresh interval of the Vault write
Set hmacSecretData: true again, because the operator ignores every rollout restart target when it does not compute a data MAC for changes
Set destination.create: true, because rollout restarts are triggered only for Kubernetes Secrets that the operator created and owns itself
Move rolloutRestartTargets into the VaultAuth resource, because restart targets are configured once for each authentication method used
